{{DISPLAYTITLE:Powerful ''p''-group}}
In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[group theory]], especially in the study of [[p-group|''p''-groups]] and [[pro-p-group|pro-''p''-groups]], the concept of '''powerful ''p''-groups''' plays an important role.  They were introduced in {{harv|Lubotzky|Mann|1987}}, where a number of applications are given, including results on [[Schur multiplier]]s.  Powerful ''p''-groups are used in the study of [[automorphism]]s of ''p''-groups {{harv|Khukhro|1998}}, the solution of the [[restricted Burnside problem]] {{harv|Vaughan-Lee|1993}}, the classification of finite ''p''-groups via the [[coclass conjectures]] {{harv|Leedham-Green|McKay|2002}}, and provided an excellent method of understanding analytic pro-''p''-groups {{harv|Dixon|du Sautoy|Mann|Segal|1991}}.

==Formal definition==
A finite ''p''-group <math>G</math> is called '''powerful''' if the [[commutator subgroup]] <math>[G,G]</math> is contained in the subgroup <math>G^p = \langle g^p | g\in G\rangle</math> for odd <math>p</math>, or if <math>[G,G]</math> is contained in the subgroup <math>G^4</math> for <math>p=2</math>.

==Properties of powerful ''p''-groups==
Powerful ''p''-groups have many properties similar to [[abelian group]]s, and thus provide a good basis for studying ''p''-groups.  Every finite ''p''-group can be expressed as a [[section (group theory)|section]] of a powerful ''p''-group.

Powerful ''p''-groups are also useful in the study of [[pro-p group|pro-''p'' groups]] as it provides a simple means for characterising [[p-adic number|''p''-adic]] analytic groups (groups that are [[manifold]]s over the ''p''-adic numbers): A finitely generated pro-''p'' group is ''p''-adic analytic if and only if it contains an [[Open set|open]] [[normal subgroup]] that is powerful: this is a special case of a deep result of [[Michel Lazard]] (1965).

Some properties similar to abelian [[p-group|''p''-groups]] are: if <math>G</math> is a powerful ''p''-group then: 
* The [[Frattini subgroup]] <math>\Phi(G)</math> of <math>G</math> has the property <math>\Phi(G) = G^p.</math>
* <math>G^{p^k} = \{g^{p^k}|g\in G\}</math> for all <math>k\geq 1.</math> That is, the ''group generated'' by <math>p</math>th powers is precisely the ''set'' of <math>p</math>th powers.
* If <math>G = \langle g_1, \ldots, g_d\rangle</math> then <math>G^{p^k} = \langle g_1^{p^k},\ldots,g_d^{p^k}\rangle</math> for all <math>k\geq 1.</math>
* The <math>k</math>th entry of the [[lower central series]] of <math>G</math> has the property <math>\gamma_k(G)\leq G^{p^{k-1}}</math> for all <math>k\geq 1.</math>
* Every [[quotient group]] of a powerful ''p''-group is powerful.
* The [[Prüfer rank]] of <math>G</math> is equal to the minimal number of generators of <math>G.</math>

Some less abelian-like properties are: if <math>G</math> is a powerful ''p''-group then: 
* <math>G^{p^k}</math> is powerful.
* [[Subgroups]] of <math>G</math> are not necessarily powerful.
